A $\triangle$ or $\bigcirc$ is placed in each of the nine squares in a 3-by-3 grid. Shown below is a sample configuration with three $\triangle$s in a line.

How many configurations will have three $\triangle$s in a line and three $\bigcirc$s in a line?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A $\triangle$ or $\bigcirc$ is placed in each of the nine squares in a 3-by-3 grid. How many configurations will have three $\triangle$s in a line and three $\bigcirc$s in a line?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: The attached image illustrates a 3-by-3 grid whose nine cells are filled with triangles or circles. For the counting problem, the relevant possible 3-cell lines in a 3-by-3 grid are the 3 rows, 3 columns, and 2 diagonals. Let n be the total number of triangle cells. To have three triangles in a line, we need n >= 3. To have three circles in a line, we need at least 3 circle cells, so n <= 6. Thus n can only be 3, 4, 5, or 6. Case n = 3: The three triangles must themselves form a line. If the triangle line is a diagonal, then every possible 3-cell line intersects that diagonal, so the six circle cells cannot contain a full circle line. Therefore the triangle line must be one of the 6 row/column lines. This gives 6 configurations. Case n = 4: The triangles must contain a 3-triangle line plus one extra triangle. Again, the 3-triangle line cannot be diagonal, since a diagonal intersects every possible circle line, leaving no full circle line among the circles. So the triangle line must be one of the 6 rows or columns. For each such line, the extra triangle can be placed in any of the 6 remaining cells. Then one of the other parallel rows or columns remains entirely circles, giving a circle line. This gives 6 * 6 = 36 configurations. There is no overcount because 4 cells cannot contain two distinct row/column 3-lines. By symmetry between triangles and circles, the n = 5 case contributes the same as n = 4, namely 36 configurations, and the n = 6 case contributes the same as n = 3, namely 6 configurations. Total: 6 + 36 + 36 + 6 = 84.

If a configuration has both a triangle-line and a circle-line, then the number of triangles must be 3, 4, 5, or 6. Case n=3: the three triangles must themselves form a line; only the 6 row/column lines work, because a diagonal line intersects every possible circle line, so its complement has no circle line. This gives 6. Case n=4: the triangles must contain a line plus one extra cell. Again the triangle line must be one of the 6 rows/columns; for each such line, the extra triangle can be any of the 6 remaining cells, and the other parallel row/column remains a circle-line. This gives 36; no overcount occurs because 4 cells cannot contain two distinct row/column 3-lines. By triangle/circle symmetry, the n=5 and n=6 cases contribute 36 and 6 respectively. Sum 6+36+36+6=84.
